analysis.one_liner: Tells the Federal Reserve to fight inflation only, dropping its legal duty to aim for maximum employment.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee voted 30-21 on May 13, 2026 to advance a bill removing employment from the Federal Reserve's legal mission, leaving price stability as the Fed's only goal; it now sits on the House calendar awaiting a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1977, the Federal Reserve's legal mission has had two parts: keep prices stable and aim for maximum employment. This bill strikes the employment half out of the law, leaving the Fed with one instruction: stable prices. In practice, that means when inflation rises, the Fed would no longer be required to weigh what its rate hikes do to jobs. Raising interest rates fights inflation partly by slowing hiring and pushing unemployment up; a Fed released from considering employment could keep rates higher for longer even as people lose work. The bill cleared its committee and is waiting for a House floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Lenders and creditors gain the most: a Fed that does not weigh employment will on average keep interest rates higher, which increases the return on loans, bonds, and savings. Asset owners also gain, because aggressive inflation-fighting protects the value of financial holdings. The bill's backers argue everyone gains from lower inflation, since high prices hit low-income households hardest — but the bill trades away the employment half of the Fed's mission to get it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill changes the Federal Reserve Act's Section 2A so the Fed's mandate reads only "stable prices" instead of "maximum employment, stable prices," removing the legal basis for the Fed to tolerate higher inflation in order to protect hiring.
For people who hold most of their wealth in money and bonds, a Fed focused single-mindedly on low inflation is the strongest possible protection for the value of what they own.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and job seekers pay, in the form of a Fed that is legally free to push unemployment higher while fighting inflation, and borrowers pay through higher rates on mortgages, credit cards, and car loans during slowdowns. The costs of a rate-tightening cycle fall first on hourly workers, renters, and small businesses, none of whom sit at the Fed's table.

drawbacks.text: With only stable prices as a goal, the Fed would be free to fight inflation by raising rates without weighing the job losses that follow — unemployment is the main tool high rates use to cool prices, and the people who lose their jobs would have no mandate provision standing in the way.

The Federal Reserve has had an employment goal written into law since 1977; removing it would be a structural change, not a tweak, and the bill's amended text leaves no substitute duty to consider the labor market.

A supporter would argue that a single price-stability mandate lowers inflation faster and inflation hurts people with small cash buffers most — the bill's backers treat that as a benefit to ordinary people, but the measure offers nothing to workers in exchange for losing the employment half of the mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's strongest good-faith case is that inflation itself hurts working people — rising grocery, rent, and gas costs fall hardest on those with least slack, and a Fed told to weigh jobs might let prices run too hot. But that case is made at a steep cost: the record on the other side, built over decades under the current dual mandate, is that recessions in which the Fed raises rates aggressively cost jobs, and those costs land on hourly workers first. The bill removes the legal counterweight to that without any replacement protection, and it does so on behalf of a monetary-policy preference held almost entirely by one party's committee majority, with two cosponsors and no broader coalition behind it.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee passed the bill on a 30-21 vote in May 2026 and reported it in June; it is now waiting on the House calendar for a floor vote, and none has been scheduled yet.

narrative.text: Rep. French Hill of Arkansas introduced the bill on September 16, 2025, joined by Reps. Stutzman and Donalds, and it was sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which Hill chairs.
The committee held a markup on May 13, 2026 and ordered the bill reported on a 30-21 vote.
On June 24, 2026 the committee reported an amended version, H. Rept. 119-710, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, which means it is waiting for House leadership to schedule a floor vote.
The bill's core change is one line of the Federal Reserve Act: the Fed's mandate language is cut down from "maximum employment, stable prices" to just "stable prices."

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the bill's supporters and the financial interests that favor a price-only Fed are ahead, because the bill cleared committee on its sponsor's home turf and is positioned for a floor vote; nothing has become law, so working people have lost nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bill's House Republican sponsors so far

for.name: Rep. French Hill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through the committee he chairs, and brought it to a 30-21 committee vote that advanced it to the House calendar.

against.name: 21 House Financial Services Committee members
against.role: Committee members who voted no in the May 13, 2026 markup
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported to the House.

sides.party_line_note: The committee's 30-21 vote to advance the bill was close to a straight party split, and both cosponsors are Republicans; the record does not list the vote's party breakdown, but the bill has no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.note: A price-only Fed will on average keep interest rates higher than a Fed that also weighs employment, and higher rates fatten the margins on loans, credit cards, and mortgages. The cost falls on borrowers, who are disproportionately ordinary households.

The wealthiest households hold most financial assets, and their value depends on low inflation. A Fed released from considering employment will fight inflation harder, which protects asset values while the resulting job losses fall on people whose main asset is a paycheck.

Higher rates raise the cost of borrowing for businesses, but a looser labor market makes workers cheaper to hire and easier to replace. The bill tilts the economy's balance toward employers and away from job seekers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Union Calendar, which is the queue for House floor votes; with the House majority held by the sponsor's party, a floor vote is plausible this session, and the narrow 30-21 committee vote suggests a close one if it comes. Even if the House passes it, the bill would then need Senate action and a presidential signature, which a two-cosponsor bill that reshapes the Fed's core mandate would find a difficult road.
